headline: AAO public guidance supports UV eye-protection counseling for outdoor sunlight exposure.
implication: Protocol safety should permit UV-blocking sunglasses/hats and advise eye-care review for ocular vulnerability or new eye symptoms.
caveat: Safety-only professional guidance.

headline: CDC heat guidance provides practical steps for modifying or avoiding outdoor activity during extreme heat.
implication: Morning outdoor-light protocols should include heat-wave modifications and an indoor-light fallback.
caveat: Safety-only guidance, not light efficacy evidence.

headline: Registry specified a six-week outdoor morning-daylight protocol of at least 30 minutes/day before 1 PM.
implication: Useful for dose/timing design and adherence tooling, but not for efficacy claims.
caveat: Terminated registry with actual enrollment of 12 and no extracted published results.

headline: Wearable light measurement is heterogeneous, and device validation/reporting gaps can limit comparability across studies.
implication: Any Murph light-exposure experiment should specify measurement device, placement, thresholds, and limitations.
caveat: Methods review only; no sleep or protocol efficacy outcome.

headline: CIE position statement gives professional guidance for proper light at the proper time.
implication: Use as external protocol/measurement context and artifact candidate; do not treat as an outdoor trial.
caveat: Position statement, not experimental evidence.

headline: CIE standard defines the metrology system underlying melanopic and α-opic light metrics.
implication: Use for terminology and measurement standards when discussing mEDI or biologically effective light.
caveat: A metrology standard is not health-outcome evidence.

headline: A 40-minute morning outdoor natural-light protocol in older adults reported significant sleep-quality improvements.
implication: Supports using outdoor daylight, not only indoor bright-light devices, as a candidate sleep experiment.
caveat: Small long-term-care sample; authors cautioned that the study cannot define a precise illuminance or duration threshold for circadian response.

headline: A 40-minute morning outdoor natural-light protocol in older adults reported significant sleep-quality improvements.
implication: Supports using outdoor daylight, not only indoor bright-light devices, as a candidate sleep experiment.
caveat: Small long-term-care sample; authors cautioned that the study cannot define a precise illuminance or duration threshold for circadian response.

headline: A 40-minute morning outdoor natural-light protocol in older adults reported significant sleep-quality improvements.
implication: Supports using outdoor daylight, not only indoor bright-light devices, as a candidate sleep experiment.
caveat: Small long-term-care sample; authors cautioned that the study cannot define a precise illuminance or duration threshold for circadian response.

headline: Bright-light treatment produced mostly mild side effects, including jitteriness, headache, nausea, and timing-related activation signals.
implication: Morning outdoor-light protocols should ask users to watch for headache, nausea, jitteriness, sleep disruption, and elevated or activated mood, especially if light exposure is intensified.
caveat: The exposure was supervised 10,000-lux artificial light for SAD, not unsupervised outdoor morning light.

headline: Simulated dawn modestly improved subjective sleep quality while in use, but effects did not persist after stopping.
implication: Useful boundary evidence for dawn-simulation sleep endpoints.
caveat: Device dawn effects should not be presented as outdoor daylight effects.

headline: Blue-enriched workplace light improved self-reported alertness, performance, mood, sleep quality, and some comfort symptoms compared with standard white light.
implication: Shows that spectral composition of daytime indoor light can change subjective sleep and alertness outcomes, but it is an indoor electric-light intervention.
caveat: Outcomes were mostly self-reported, expectation effects were possible, and the exposure was workplace electric lighting rather than outdoor daylight.

headline: Scheduled bright light shifted circadian phase but generally did not outperform scheduled dim light for insomnia outcomes.
implication: Use as a cautionary clinical-boundary source showing that phase shifting alone does not guarantee sleep improvement.
caveat: The trial used indoor light boxes plus sleep-hygiene sessions in older adults with primary insomnia; it is not direct evidence for outdoor morning-light habits.

headline: Scheduled bright light shifted circadian phase but generally did not outperform scheduled dim light for insomnia outcomes.
implication: Use as a cautionary clinical-boundary source showing that phase shifting alone does not guarantee sleep improvement.
caveat: The trial used indoor light boxes plus sleep-hygiene sessions in older adults with primary insomnia; it is not direct evidence for outdoor morning-light habits.

headline: Brief report title and indexed metadata indicate subjective sleep quality improved with natural-light exposure in nursing-home residents.
implication: Adds direct natural-light sleep-quality context, but it is not enough to set protocol details.
caveat: Accessible PubMed/metadata pages do not provide sample size, full comparator details, dose, or adverse-event extraction.

headline: Brief report title and indexed metadata indicate subjective sleep quality improved with natural-light exposure in nursing-home residents.
implication: Adds direct natural-light sleep-quality context, but it is not enough to set protocol details.
caveat: Accessible PubMed/metadata pages do not provide sample size, full comparator details, dose, or adverse-event extraction.

headline: Brief report title and indexed metadata indicate subjective sleep quality improved with natural-light exposure in nursing-home residents.
implication: Adds direct natural-light sleep-quality context, but it is not enough to set protocol details.
caveat: Accessible PubMed/metadata pages do not provide sample size, full comparator details, dose, or adverse-event extraction.

headline: Light and walking arms improved short-term actigraphic wake time in AD, but benefits were not sustained at 6 months and light was not morning outdoor exposure.
implication: Useful clinical bundle/boundary evidence, especially for adherence and safety notes, but not direct support for a general morning outdoor protocol.
caveat: Clinical AD population; light was artificial and timed before bedtime, not outdoor morning light.

headline: Evening-type student workers reported poorer sleep and fatigue and had lower moderate waking light, while objective sleep parameters did not differ by chronotype.
implication: Real-world light patterns may differ by chronotype, but objective sleep findings were not uniformly positive.
caveat: Young student-worker population and chronotype comparison are adjacent to, not direct evidence for, a morning outdoor-light protocol.

headline: Natural light-dark exposure can entrain human circadian timing, but the intervention is not a brief morning-only protocol.
implication: Supports the mechanism that outdoor daylight and low evening light can alter circadian timing.
caveat: The natural-light field condition bundles full-day light, darkness, activity, and environmental changes.

headline: Afternoon-shift students slept longer and were less sleepy but had lower light exposure than morning-shift students.
implication: Morning light may interact with schedule and chronotype, but school timing and adolescent biology limit translation.
caveat: Adolescent school-shift context is a population and schedule mismatch for adult morning outdoor-light practice.

headline: Delayed sleepers showed more light/activity in the biological night and less morning light/activity than controls.
implication: Supports a timing-sensitive view of light exposure, especially avoiding late-night light and considering morning light in delayed sleepers.
caveat: Clinical delayed-sleep population; observational comparisons do not prove morning light treatment efficacy.

headline: Season and weekend natural-light patterns can influence circadian and sleep timing.
implication: Supports implementation caveats that season, latitude, and evening light shape morning-light dose meaning.
caveat: Not a randomized test of a brief outdoor morning protocol.

headline: Five days of direct morning sunlight exposure improved global subjective sleep quality in older nursing-home residents.
implication: Supports testing a simple outdoor morning-light habit as a sleep-quality intervention signal.
caveat: Short institutional older-adult study; accessible abstract does not provide detailed adverse-event reporting or a general-adult estimate.

headline: Five days of direct morning sunlight exposure improved global subjective sleep quality in older nursing-home residents.
implication: Supports testing a simple outdoor morning-light habit as a sleep-quality intervention signal.
caveat: Short institutional older-adult study; accessible abstract does not provide detailed adverse-event reporting or a general-adult estimate.

caveat: Short institutional older-adult study; accessible abstract does not provide detailed adverse-event reporting or a general-adult estimate.

headline: Five days of direct morning sunlight exposure improved global subjective sleep quality in older nursing-home residents.
implication: Supports testing a simple outdoor morning-light habit as a sleep-quality intervention signal.
caveat: Short institutional older-adult study; accessible abstract does not provide detailed adverse-event reporting or a general-adult estimate.

headline: Older adults had much lower morning and bright-light exposure in winter than summer, while sleep-quality differences were not statistically detected.
implication: Seasonal feasibility constraints can be large in care settings, but not every health endpoint changes clearly.
caveat: Small exploratory older-adult care-home study; not a general-population protocol trial.

headline: The historical review estimated low aggregate mania/hypomania switch rates after light therapy but identified rapid cycling and assessment method as important caveats.
implication: Morning outdoor-light guidance should include a bipolar/mania screening boundary and monitoring for elevated mood, reduced need for sleep, agitation, or mixed symptoms.
caveat: The review addresses clinical light therapy for bipolar depression, not outdoor-morning-light wellness use.

headline: Photophobia is a clinical condition where light exposure can cause pain or substantial discomfort.
implication: Outdoor-light protocols should include a photophobia/migraine off-ramp and avoid requiring direct exposure in bright conditions.
caveat: Safety-only, not an efficacy source.

headline: DSWPD participants had less phase-advancing light exposure relative to circadian timing despite complex clock-time patterns.
implication: Morning-light protocols should consider biological timing, not just clock time, especially in delayed sleepers.
caveat: Small clinical sample; relative circadian timing in DSWPD is not the same as default healthy-adult outdoor morning exposure.

headline: Management review translates drug-induced photosensitivity into practical diagnosis, prevention, and management concerns.
implication: Protocol pages should include a photosensitizing-medication caution and avoid giving individualized medication advice.
caveat: Use as a safety boundary; do not infer that all sunlight exposure is contraindicated for every listed drug.

headline: Photosensitizing medications warrant screening before elective light exposure.
implication: Use to justify medication screening, conservative pause/clinician review language, and stop rules for sunburn-like reactions.
caveat: Do not assume every listed medication reacts to red/NIR wavelengths; use as conservative screening only.

headline: Melanopic illuminance is a key metric for circadian light-response magnitude.
implication: Supports use of melanopic dose language instead of relying only on photopic lux.
caveat: Metric validation/analysis; not an outdoor behavior intervention.

headline: Athlete travel intervention evidence is limited and not cleanly light-isolated.
implication: Use to preserve uncertainty around jet-lag/light countermeasures.
caveat: Systematic review across heterogeneous interventions and sport settings.

headline: The healthy-adult personal-light evidence base was limited, low quality, and mixed/conflicting across sleep and mood outcomes.
implication: Protocol synthesis should avoid overclaiming observational personal-light literature and should distinguish endpoints.
caveat: Review-level background; not a direct morning outdoor-light intervention review.

headline: More habitual outdoor daylight time was associated with fewer insomnia/tiredness symptoms and earlier chronotype in UK Biobank.
implication: Supports tracking outdoor-light exposure and sleep/circadian outcomes, not causal claims.
caveat: Self-reported exposure, not morning-specific, and observational.

headline: More habitual outdoor daylight time was associated with fewer insomnia/tiredness symptoms and earlier chronotype in UK Biobank.
implication: Supports tracking outdoor-light exposure and sleep/circadian outcomes, not causal claims.
caveat: Self-reported exposure, not morning-specific, and observational.

headline: Indoor daylight access at home stabilized circadian timing and improved selected sleep and mood measures, while some sleep endpoints were unchanged.
implication: Supports the same circadian-light mechanism behind morning outdoor light, but the exposure was indoor daylight through residential glazing rather than outdoor light.
caveat: Context-only for the outdoor protocol: small healthy sample, residential/window intervention, short intervention windows, and electric-light context not fully controlled.

headline: Morning blue-enriched light improved daytime sleepiness in a small insomnia pilot, while objective sleep and circadian biomarkers were not significant.
implication: Use as directly adjacent morning-light clinical evidence with strong sample-size and modality caveats.
caveat: Indoor device-based blue-enriched light at 380 lux in a 14-person open-label trial is not direct evidence for outdoor morning light exposure.

headline: Brighter post-wake light related to lower morning sleepiness, while higher pre-bedtime light related to longer sleep onset latency.
implication: Suggests Murph users should track both morning/daytime light and evening-light contamination.
caveat: Small convenience sample; not outdoor-only and not a protocol intervention.

headline: Morning sunlight, relative to no sunlight, predicted better next-night subjective sleep quality; duration generally did not.
implication: Supports timing-focused tracking in an N-of-1 habit experiment.
caveat: Self-reported diary study; not randomized and not necessarily outdoor-only or objective light measurement.

headline: Morning sunlight, relative to no sunlight, predicted better next-night subjective sleep quality; duration generally did not.
implication: Supports timing-focused tracking in an N-of-1 habit experiment.
caveat: Self-reported diary study; not randomized and not necessarily outdoor-only or objective light measurement.

headline: Morning sunlight, relative to no sunlight, predicted better next-night subjective sleep quality; duration generally did not.
implication: Supports timing-focused tracking in an N-of-1 habit experiment.
caveat: Self-reported diary study; not randomized and not necessarily outdoor-only or objective light measurement.

headline: Morning/daytime light was linked with better sleep indices in athletes, but evening light was linked with worse sleep-behavior scores.
implication: Supports light-timing endpoints and evening-light caution in adjacent athletic populations.
caveat: Small homogeneous male athlete sample; observational and not outdoor-only.

headline: Elite-sport sleep intervention evidence includes light therapy but remains heterogeneous.
implication: Useful for athlete evidence-base context, not as a direct morning outdoor-light claim.
caveat: Systematic review across heterogeneous interventions; light therapy is not isolated to outdoor morning exposure.

headline: ISBD clinical recommendations emphasize anti-manic prophylaxis, conservative titration, and monitoring when using light therapy in bipolar disorder.
implication: Morning outdoor-light instructions should warn people with bipolar disorder, recent mania/hypomania, mixed symptoms, or rapid cycling to seek clinician guidance before deliberate light-dosing changes.
caveat: This is a clinical bright-light therapy guideline, not an efficacy source for outdoor morning light.

headline: Morning sunlight before 10 AM was associated with earlier sleep midpoint and lower PSQI score, while several sleep parameters were null.
implication: Supports using sleep timing and subjective quality as outcomes in a morning sunlight experiment.
caveat: Cross-sectional, self-reported, and collected during the COVID-19 pandemic period; no causal inference.

headline: Morning sunlight before 10 AM was associated with earlier sleep midpoint and lower PSQI score, while several sleep parameters were null.
implication: Supports using sleep timing and subjective quality as outcomes in a morning sunlight experiment.
caveat: Cross-sectional, self-reported, and collected during the COVID-19 pandemic period; no causal inference.

headline: Morning sunlight before 10 AM was associated with earlier sleep midpoint and lower PSQI score, while several sleep parameters were null.
implication: Supports using sleep timing and subjective quality as outcomes in a morning sunlight experiment.
caveat: Cross-sectional, self-reported, and collected during the COVID-19 pandemic period; no causal inference.

headline: A large behavior bundle including morning sunlight was associated with improved sleep consistency and cardiorespiratory metrics.
implication: Useful for real-world behavior-bundle context, but morning sunlight cannot be separated from eating, exercise, and breathwork behaviors.
caveat: Pre-post quasi-experimental design with self-selection and bundled behaviors; not a randomized light-only study.

headline: Less time in bright light was associated with more sleep-wake fragmentation, but afternoon timing—not morning timing—best discriminated consolidation in older men.
implication: Supports outdoor/daytime bright-light exposure while preserving a timing caveat for morning-only recommendations.
caveat: Cross-sectional older-men cohort; not an intervention and not generalizable to all users.

headline: Season and geographic location strongly influenced human illumination exposure, mediated by indoor/outdoor behavior.
implication: Morning outdoor-light dose is modified by latitude, season, and behavior, not merely by prescription duration.
caveat: Naturalistic illumination monitoring; not an intervention.

headline: In a short-term 10,000-lux light-therapy report, side effects were common but mostly mild and transient.
implication: Protocol safety language can mention headache and eye/vision symptoms as things to watch when increasing light intensity or duration.
caveat: The exposure was artificial 10,000-lux treatment, not outdoor morning light.

headline: The WHO Global Solar UV Index gives a public-health framework for deciding when outdoor light needs sun-protection boundaries.
implication: Morning outdoor-light instructions should distinguish circadian light exposure from unnecessary UV exposure and use the UV Index for protection decisions.
caveat: The guide supports safety framing only, not efficacy claims for morning light.

headline: WHO UV guidance distinguishes beneficial small UV exposure from excessive UV risk and recommends protection at UVI 3 or above.
implication: Outdoor-light protocols should not equate more sun with better outcomes; use UV Index and protection measures.
caveat: Safety-only public-health guidance.
